2vq5t8:298: In 2008, Clay Shirky noted in "Here Comes Everybody" that the internet drove coordination costs to near zero, causing institutional functions to begin leaking into ad hoc groups — Wikipedia replaced the Encyclopaedia Britannica, flash mobs arose, and coordination without organization became possible. The author argues that 18 years later, we are doing the same thing with a different cost curve: this time it is a story of "building," not "coordinating." Building complex software once required a software company — engineers, build processes, UI design stages, and JIRA ticket management. Agentic programming tools, MCP, and headless platforms are compressing building costs dramatically: a finance lead can spin up a reconciliation agent on Tuesday afternoon, and a recruiter can assemble a candidate research workflow while sipping coffee.

6dr86y:283: The author cites the 1917 founding of Piggly Wiggly in Memphis by Clarence Saunders as an example of this "labor outsourcing" model: in the 1920s, grocery stores shifted from the clerk-retrieval model to the open-shelf model, where customers selected items themselves. This process went through multiple capability unlocks — open-shelf layouts, UPC barcodes, cheap touchscreens — and each wave was marketed with "convenience" as the selling point. The "self-service" process in enterprise software is similar: vendors externalize configuration work to customers, and customers must hire or cultivate talent capable of navigating these "raw materials." The difference is that grocery shopping is a voluntary choice, while enterprise software choices are often passive — businesses cannot choose not to use Salesforce, but they must bear the cost of implementing it.
